newsitem.title: USA: NYC balances books but faces big risks toward 2000.
newsitem.headline: NYC balances books but faces big risks toward 2000.

text.p: New York City used banner profits by Wall Street firms to shore up its proposed fiscal year 1998 budget, but the Guiliani Administration's new plan still has big risks, especially in later years, bond analysts said on Thursday.
Mayor Rudolph Giuliani proposed a preliminary $32.9 budget for fiscal 1998 that seeks to use a nearly $1.2 billion surplus to satisfy key constituencies as he heads into an election year.
Parents will see spending on schools rise $500 million through 1999.

Residents, who had an opportunity to splurge on clothing during a recent, one-week break on sales taxes, can look forward to seeing the city's share of this tax eliminated by year-end, if Albany agrees.
Businesses also will benefit from tax breaks, like ending or reducing the unicorporated business tax and cutting commercial rent taxes.

And rating agencies and fiscal monitors saluted the Giuliani Administration for trying to balance the city's books in fiscal 1998 with $491 million of this year's surplus, including using $391 million to pre-pay debt.
While Giuliani admitted Wall Street's near-record profits served the city well, he also pointed to his Administration's ability to rein in spending at a City Hall news conference.
"Luck is very often the residue of design and in this case, it's an equal combination of both."

But even with the unusual cushion of surplus funds, the Giuliani Administration still projects a $2.4 billion budget gap in fiscal 1998, followed by a nearly $3.3 billion gap in 2000. And the city remains vulnerable to any downturn in the economy or at Wall Street's powerhouse banks and brokerages, all points fiscal monitors highlighted.
The New York State comptroller, in prepared remarks, said: "I welcome his (Giuliani's) commitment to address and not simply talk about structural balance.
"However, the budget gaps in fiscal 1999-2001 still remain formidable," McCall said.

Bob Kurtter, an analyst with Moody's Investors Service, noted that the city is relying upon Gov George Pataki succeeding in getting big reductions in Medicaid spending approved, which Albany lawmakers have failed to agree to in the past, as well as the economy's continued strength.
"So they're not out of the woods yet, even though I feel their economy is strong and stable at this point."

Another potential trouble spot was identified by a Standard & Poor's Corp analyst, who even though he said his initial reaction was positive, noted that the Giuliani Administration plan to boost capital spending, though modest, has a stiff cost.
"Overall debt levels for the city are high and we're very concerned they're going to get too high," said Martin Arrick, who also pointed to big, out-year gaps as cause for concern.
The plan would sharply increase the city's cost of debt service, as it would rise to nearly 19 percent in fiscal 1999 from about 16.5 percent in fiscal 1997.
While debt service would ease after that, slipping a few percentage points in 2000, it would climb again by 2002, when the mayor projected it would reach almost 19.5 percent.
But Arrick added that at first glance, he did not see anything in the mayor's preliminary plan that would cause him to change the city's rating.
Standard and Poor's rates New York BBB-plus with a stable outlook, he added.
Instead of running up its debt service, the Moody's analyst suggested that the city might be better served by relying more heavily on pay-as-you-go financing instead.
((--U.S. Municipal Desk, 212-859-1650))
